description.narrative:
Over the past few decades, microfinance has become a dominant development strategy around the world to provide a range of services,its main business is lending credit, purportedly to reduce poverty, empower women, improve well-being, or a combination ofthese goals that including Cambodia. Mostly the northeastern provinces of Cambodia including Ratanakiri, Mondulkiri, Kratie, and Stung Trengprovinces are home to a high concentration of indigenous peoples and rural farming communities. These areas are characterized by geographic isolation, limited infrastructure, and low access to public services, including legal aid, education, and financial institutions. Livelihoods rely heavily on small-scale agriculture, forest products, and seasonal labor, making households vulnerable to income fluctuations. In Cambodia, microfinance emerged in the 1990s out of international efforts to alleviate poverty through market-based strategies which consisted of donor-funded NGOs that disbursed credit to microenterprises through group-lending methods. By the end of the decade, however, microﬁnance operated by NGOs began to transform into commercial institutions (Micro Financial Institutions – MFIs) with the assistance of Western development partners such as FMO, AFD, KfW and Oikocredit. The MFIs proceeded rapidly during the 2000s, as a result, MFIs switched from group lending to individual loan with issued land titles. Attracted by fast growth rates and proﬁtable returns, regional banks from East Asia have recently acquired majority shares in Cambodia’s largest MFIs. Based on NBC report in 2021, the Financial Institutions (FIs) consist of 7 Commercial Banks with small-loan portfolios, 5 deposit-taking MFIs, 79 small MFIs, and 234 rural credit institutions. Borrowers applyloans from MFIs by using property (national ID card, land plot, housing, vehicles) as collateral. The loan came along with a payment scheme and interest, depending on length of payment and amount of the loan. According to the Cambodia Microfinance Association (CMA), microfinance institutions (MFIs) had 3.06 million active loansacross 3.6 million households nationwide in 2022, with the majority of these loans secured by land or asset-based collateral. The loan from MFIs (micro- and small-loan portfolio)increased from US$ 98 million in 2004 to more than US$ 16.4 billion in 2022, equivalent to more than 60% of the GDP . NGO Finding Reports - Debt threat report by LICADHO and Equitable Cambodia The Debt Threat Researchpublished in August 2023, was commissioned by The Cambodian League for the Promotion and Defense of Human Rights (LICADHO) and Equitable Cambodia (EC) released some key findings. Most borrowers in Cambodia face severe over-indebtedness, with over two-thirds acknowledging excessive householddebt and more than a quarter spending over 70% of their income on repayments far exceeding ethical lending standards. Disturbingly, about 10% spend more than they earn, forcing harmful sacrifices like eating less, withdrawing children from school, or selling land. Since over 92% of borrowers must provide land titles as collateral for microloans, debt-driven land sales are common, affecting both agricultural and residential properties. Additionally, some children drop out of school or work to repay loans,and nearly one-fifth of households eat less after borrowing. Borrowers increasingly take new loans to repay existing debts,with over a third of 2022 loans used this way, signaling unsustainable debt levels. Despite widespread collateral use, most borrowers do not expect formal legal foreclosure, reflecting poor awareness of their rights and irregular, often informal, land seizure practices. To meet their debt obligations, families frequently cut back on essential expenses such as food, leading to increased food insecurity and malnutrition. When access to formal microfinance is limited, many borrowers turn to informal lenders or loan sharks, where they face exorbitant interest rates and even harsher repayment terms. Microfinance sectors have grown atan unprecedented pace, leading to concerns about over-indebtedness and financial risks. The fact that the average loan size exceeded 95% of incomes in 2021highlights the extent to which households have relied on credit, often beyond their repayment capacity. Following a complaint submitted by a group of NGOs to the EU and OECD regarding Cambodia’s debt crisis, calls for stricter investment regulations and enhanced oversight of financial institutions have intensified. In response, the UN Resident Coordinator in Cambodia, alongside European financial investors; including IFC, FMO, KfW, Belgium Bank, NBC, ABC, and CMA; established a high-level coordination committee to addressthe issue. Oxfam in Cambodia has been representing civil society organizations (CSOs)within this committee. The committee's effortshave led to significant progress. The National Bank of Cambodia (NBC), as the sector regulator, has strengthened enforcement of loan policies for private banks and MFIs, improving financial institutions'overall performance. Notable developments include stricter loan approval processes, the introduction of stronger client protection policies across financial institutions, the establishment of formal complaint mechanisms for borrowers, and increased financial literacy training for the public.
Impact: Rural and indigenous communities, especially women, are financially resilient and empowered, safeguarded from exploitative lending practices, and activelyengaged in inclusive and equitable economic development." Project Goal: To promote inclusive and equitable economic development by strengthening the resilience of rural and indigenous communities particularly women through improved access to fair debt resolution mechanisms, enhanced financial literacy, andstrengthened institutional capacity of the National Authority for Alternative Dispute Resolution (NADR) to address financial disputes effectively. Outcomes: 1. Increased access to fair and free indebtedness redress mechanisms for vulnerable groups, indigenous communities, and especially women borrowers. 2. Enhanced capacity of NADR to effectively implement gender-sensitive and inclusive alternative dispute resolution (ADR) mechanisms in the financial sector. 3. Improved financialliteracy among ruralandindigenous communities, resulting in better household financial management, reduced over-indebtedness, and participation in inclusive economic opportunities.

participating-org.narrative: Oxfam Novib is one of the 17 national affiliates of the Oxfam International Confederation. It started life in 1956 as the Netherlands Organisation for International Assistance (Novib), and joined forces with Oxfam in 1994. Working together in confederation, the Oxfam affiliates can speak with one clear and compelling voice on issues of global concern: climate change, health and education forall, agriculture, trade, and conflicts and emergencies. Oxfam established this country office to support local organizations and projects. Through this local office Oxfam Novib directly contributes towards this project#s implementation.
